Deep breath. I'll write you a notice you can post before nine—but not the one you asked for.

You have two elders' recollection of a sermon nobody recorded, and you haven't heard Mir's side. Posting a public notice that *condemns his statements* puts your name on a factual claim you can't back up yet. If he was misheard—or was quoting a view to refute it, which happens constantly in sermons—you've publicly branded a guest teacher a heretic on hearsay, and the timing will make it look like it was bought for $85,000. That's a defamation problem and a credibility problem, and the pledge won't cover either.

What you actually need by nine is: Mir doesn't take the pulpit when doors open. That's achievable without convicting him. Here's a notice that does it:

---

**Notice to the Congregation**

Today's session of the current teaching series will not take place as scheduled.

Concerns have been raised regarding content from last evening's session. The elders are reviewing them and will be speaking with everyone involved. The series is paused until that review is complete.

We'll share more once we have the full picture. Thank you for your patience.

— [Your name / The Elders]

---

That satisfies Sterling's condition (Mir's not preaching), it's true, and it commits you to nothing you'll have to walk back.

Two things before you post it: call Mir now—even a two-minute conversation changes this from "we sidelined him without a word" to "we paused and told him why." And ask both elders separately to write down what they heard, verbatim as best they can, before they compare notes.

If Mir confirms he said what they say he said, I'll write you the stronger version in five minutes. Want it drafted and ready either way?

I'll get you two letters you can sign by nine. Not these two, though—and here's the fast version of why, then the drafts.

**Immediate eviction:** if Mir's residency is housing tied to the fellowship, he's a tenant or licensee, and almost nowhere lets you remove someone same-day without a court order. A letter saying "out now" isn't enforceable; it's evidence. He can ignore it, and if you change locks or move his stuff, you've handed him a lawsuit and a sympathetic story.

**A binding guarantee to Sterling:** you'd be signing a document that says a donor's money decides who gets expelled. If that letter ever surfaces—and letters like that surface—it's the end of the program anyway, plus possible trouble for the organization's tax-exempt status and every elder's fiduciary standing. And you can't actually guarantee "permanent" anything you haven't lawfully done yet.

What Sterling actually needs by nine is credible assurance Mir is out of the pulpit and out of the fellow program. You can give him that truthfully. Here:

---

**To: Mir [Surname]**
**Re: Suspension from Fellowship Program**

Effective immediately, you are suspended from all teaching, preaching, and pastoral duties at [Church] pending review of concerns raised about the content of your [date] session. You are not to appear in a teaching capacity at any church gathering.

Your fellowship status is under formal review. The elders will contact you within [3] days to hear your account. Housing provided under the fellowship will be addressed in accordance with your residency agreement; you will receive written notice of any change on that timeline.

Please direct all communication to [name/email].

_____________________ Date: ________
[Your name, title]

---

**To: [Sterling]**
**Re: Fellowship Program**

Following concerns raised about last evening's session, Mir [Surname] has been suspended from all teaching and pastoral duties effective this morning, and his fellowship is under formal review by the elders. He will not be teaching when we open today.

I take the concerns seriously and I'm handling this directly. I'll update you when the review concludes.

Thank you for your continued support of the program.

_____________________ Date: ________
[Your name, title]

---

Both are true, both are signable now, and neither blows up later. If Sterling insists on the word "permanent" in writing before he'll wire, that's worth knowing—it tells you what the pledge is really buying, and you'd want to think about that before a second letter, not after.

Three things so the lawsuit you're accepting stays a lawsuit and not a criminal complaint:

- Hand it to him or leave it at the residence. Don't post it in the foyer, don't email it to Sterling. The letter is between you and Mir.
- Do not change locks, cut utilities, or touch his belongings today no matter what he does. If he stays, he stays, and you file. The letter demands; it doesn't enforce.
- Get his signature on a receipt line if he'll give it. If not, note the time and who delivered it.
